source: Klein, Jalaeian, Hoffman & Mueller (2023) The plausibility transition model for sensemaking, re-read for trigger rules
finding: Re-read for gap 2. The paper gives no numeric rule for anomalies, strain, frame abandonment, number of frames or number of hypotheses. Anomalies are violated expectancies. Strain is qualitative. Story building stops when plausibility is experienced as sufficient.
numbers: Corpus 73 cases (convenience sample); 23 analysed; coded by one reviewer (the senior author). Literature search 1,042 hits, 18 strongly relevant, 22 used. No participants, no statistics. Only count of rival stories: 2 (USS Vincennes).
quote: We detect anomalies when our expectancies are violated.
limits: Page text read to character 100000 of 104726. Qualitative case coding by one person. No '3 frames' limit appears here, so that number must come from the 2007 chapter, which is still unopened.
agent_relevance: A trigger rule has to be our own design choice (for example a strain counter with a tuned threshold). The theory gives no number to copy. Treat any threshold as a parameter to measure.

source: Klein, Phillips, Rall & Peluso (2007) A data-frame theory of sensemaking; and FOCUS report (Sieck et al. 2007): access attempts
finding: Gap 2 not closed. The DTIC FOCUS report returned HTTP 403 on the HTML and PDF routes, and curl got an HTML block page. Search snippets confirm the six frame activities (elaborate, question, compare, preserve, reframe, seek) and nothing on a 3-frame limit.
numbers: None obtained.
limits: Founding chapter and the FOCUS report both remain unread. All claims about D/F rules stay second hand.
agent_relevance: Do not cite 'up to 3 frames' or '3-4 anchors' as a rule. Use as a design hint only.

source: Shidara et al. (2026) Advances in LLM Reasoning Enable Flexibility in Clinical Problem-Solving (mARC)
finding: Gap 4. On the same 100-item Einstellung benchmark, newer reasoning models match or pass 5 physicians. Best model Claude 4.1 Opus 0.751 (CI 0.738-0.763) vs physicians 0.66 (CI 0.55-0.75). Four models were not significantly different from physicians.
numbers: 100 author-written items; 15 stochastic trials per model; 5 physicians (2 h limit). Human-miss subset 20 items (3 or more of 5 wrong): humans 36% (CI 26-46) vs 73% on the rest. Claude 4.1 Opus on that subset: decisively correct 55.0%, decisively wrong 25.0%, indeterminate 20.0%.
limits: Same group and same benchmark family as Kim 2025, so not independent. Only 100 items and 5 physicians; the 20-item subset has wide intervals. The abstract's '55% to 70%' is not supported in the body text, only 55% is. Authors say construct validation of Einstellung is pending. Per-model reasoning vs non-reasoning gaps are only in a figure.
agent_relevance: Fixation on a familiar pattern seems to fade with model generation on this benchmark. Still, 25% decisively wrong on the hardest items means a frame-check step may not be needed on average but is needed for the tail.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Limitations of LLMs in Clinical Problem-Solving Arising from Inflexible Reasoning (M-ARC), re-read
finding: Gap 4 baseline. Dec 2024 models scored under 50% on M-ARC; the best, Gemini-1.5-Pro, got 50%, o1 got 48%. Physicians got 66% (SE 5.3). Models were overconfident.
numbers: 100 questions; 5 physicians 66%; Gemini-1.5-Pro 50%; o1 48%; several models under 20%; 15 samples per question for consistency; model cutoff 19 Dec 2024.
limits: Questions written by the authors and screened by physician majority, not filtered against LLMs, so selection bias against models is not described. Authors say items are unlikely in real practice.
agent_relevance: Taken with d03: 50% (best, Dec 2024) to 75% (best, 2026) on the same item family. A generation effect is the simplest reading, but no independent fixation benchmark has repeated this.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky & Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify, full text re-read for gap 5
finding: Eleven LLMs, Wason-style rule discovery. Success ranged 6% to 78% within 45 turns. Think-in-Opposites raised task success in all 11 model settings; Dual-Goal in 8 of 11. Both raised the disconfirming-to-confirming test ratio (I:C) in 18 of 22 cases. Gains were significant for thinking-mode models and mixed for non-thinking models.
numbers: Mean rule discovery 42% to 56%. Human baseline cited: 29 participants, 21 found the rule; I:C 1.79 for first-attempt success vs 0.24. Non-thinking models capped at 256 new tokens per turn; thinking models up to 16K per turn. Each point averaged over 80 episodes (192 on Blicket).
limits: Rule discovery with a binary oracle, not open diagnosis. Authors say generalisation to naturalistic reasoning is future work. Token cost of the intervention itself is not isolated. Thinking-mode gain over non-thinking was not explained by lower confirmation bias.
agent_relevance: A forced disconfirming test step is cheap to add and helps where the oracle gives yes or no feedback. It helps less if the model cannot think before acting.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Blicket transfer table
finding: Transfer to a causal object task (Blicket test) was tested. TiO prompting raised Qwen3-32B from 0.57 to 0.86 and Qwen3-8B from 0.32 to 0.40. Distilled students transferred only part of the gain.
numbers: Qwen3-32B Base 0.57 / TiO 0.86, I:C 0.54 to 1.31; Qwen3-8B Base 0.32 / TiO 0.40. Student 8B from 8B-TiO 0.34, from 32B-TiO 0.36-0.38; student 32B from 32B-TiO 0.77. Dual-Goal not tested here because a Blicket hypothesis has no clean opposite.
limits: Still a rule-discovery game with an oracle. 'Opposite' is undefined for open hypotheses, which is the exact case in debugging or diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Disconfirming-test prompts move one step beyond numbers (to objects) but the open-task step is untested. The undefined-opposite problem is the real obstacle.

source: Branchini, Burro & Bianchi (2023) Training people to think in opposites facilitates the falsification process in Wason's rule discovery task
finding: A short training to list properties of the seed triple, name their opposites and test an opposite raised rule discovery in humans from 36.7% to 78.3%.
numbers: N=120, 60 per group. Training 47/60 found the rule, control 22/60; chi2(1, N=120)=22.067, p<.001, R2=0.178. Correct on attempt 1: training 27 of 47 solvers, control 3 of 22. Descending triple tried: 95% vs 60%. Training took longer (F(1,67)=10.63, p=.002).
limits: Training bundles three phases, so the opposites step is not isolated. Single task, psychology students, training took more time. Page read to 100000 of 124286 characters.
agent_relevance: Source of the forced-opposite operator. Cost is more time per decision, which for an agent means more tokens.

source: Branchini, Bianchi & Burro (2025) Thinking in opposites improves hypothesis testing performance in Wason's rule-discovery task (Memory & Cognition)
finding: A three-arm follow-up isolates the opposites step. Properties-only training did not help; opposites training did.
numbers: N=180, 60 per group. Solved: opposites 78.33%, properties-only 38.33%, control 36.66%; chi2(2, N=180)=27.986, p<.001. TO and TP took longer than control. TO did not submit more triples.
limits: One task. Authors state conclusions about hypothesis testing in general are 'not tenable at this stage' and ask for tests in medical diagnosis and other real domains. Time not equated.
agent_relevance: The disconfirming step carries the gain, not just thinking harder. Direct transfer to diagnosis is still unmeasured in humans and in LLMs.

source: LLM-as-an-Investigator: Evidence-First Agentic Reasoning for Robust Interactive Problem Diagnosis (Solution Investigator Agent, SIA), arXiv 2606.13220
finding: Open troubleshooting task (303 forum threads; 100 scored cases). An agent that keeps competing hypotheses, runs a counterfactual critique and asks follow-up questions beats ReAct, ToT and plain reasoning. This is the closest test of a forced disconfirming step on open diagnosis.
numbers: Final score: SIA 79.2 [72.7, 83.7]; THK-int 72.8; Ask-5 72.3; ReAct 69.0; ToT 61.5; BAS 67.3; THK 67.5. Ablation of final score: no counterfactual critique 74.0, no structured investigation 72.8, no hypothesis expansion 76.5, no follow-up questions 75.0, no adjudication 76.0. Hypotheses held: SIA 9.0, ReAct 12.7, ToT 21.0, BAS 4.3. Misleading user hint (10 paired cases): final 80.0 to 76.0; wrong cause chosen in 2 of 10; exact diagnosis 6/10 to 5/10.
limits: Token and API cost are not reported, so there is no equal-token comparison. LLM-judged scores, user simulator, 100 cases, stress test only 10 pairs.
agent_relevance: Best sign that a counterfactual step helps on open diagnosis (about 5 points). Cost unknown. A large hypothesis set is not better by itself: ToT held 21 hypotheses and scored worst.

source: Preventing Premature Commitment in Coding Agents with an Evidence-Conditioned Execution Layer (ECLoop), arXiv 2607.28815
finding: A gate that holds an edit or patch until stated evidence conditions are met raised SWE-bench Verified pass@1 and cut tokens. Structured conditions beat a natural-language summary of the same conditions.
numbers: 500 instances, 2 models, 2 scaffolds. mini-swe-agent GPT-5-mini 56.2 to 68.0 (+11.8); MiniMax-M2.5 75.8 to 80.6 (+4.8); Codex CLI GPT-5-mini 40.4 to 50.8; MiniMax 74.8 to 79.8 (+5.0). Tokens per instance 179K to 157K (-12.1%), 219K to 206K, 111K to 105K, 165K to 162K. Ablation (100 items, GPT-5-mini): full 68, no guidance 63, no commitment check 58, no evidence-state update 59, NL summary instead of structured 58, baseline 47. A held action is retried at most 3 times, then an audited fallback.
limits: Same model writes the conditions and acts, so shared blind spots. Only SWE-bench Verified. Conditions depend on issue quality. It gates edits, not frames.
agent_relevance: A measured commit rule: do not commit until a checklist of expected observations is satisfied. Closest thing to a stopping rule for gap 7, and it saved tokens. Structured state beat prose state by 10 of 100.

source: Think Locally, Explain Globally (EoG): graph-guided LLM investigations with controller-held belief tracking, arXiv 2601.17915
finding: On root-cause diagnosis, an LLM that only mines local evidence while a deterministic controller holds the belief state beats ReAct by a wide margin and is far more consistent. Telling ReAct to follow the same algorithm in prose did not help.
numbers: ITBench SRE, 35 scenarios x 3 runs. maj@3 F1: GPT-5.1 ReAct 8.6 vs EoG 86.1; GPT-OSS-120B 5.7 vs 79.4; Gemini 3 Flash 74.3 vs 92.1; Kimi K2 28.6 vs 83.0. ReAct prompted with the EoG algorithm: maj@3 recall 2.9 (GPT-5.1), 0.0 (Gemini 3 Flash), 0.0 (Kimi K2). Output tokens EoG about 2K vs 3.8K-21.2K; input tokens higher for EoG on three of four models.
limits: Small, one domain, preprint, work in progress. ReAct had more tools. The belief state sits outside the model, not in its context. LLM judge. No ablation isolating explicit belief tracking beyond the prompt-only arm.
agent_relevance: Evidence that an explicit hypothesis state held by code, not only prose, matters a lot. The prompt-only arm failing is a warning that writing a frame object into the context may not be enough.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam & Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong: An Analysis of Iterative Prompting for Reasoning Problems, arXiv 2310.12397
finding: Gap 3. On graph coloring, self-critique made GPT-4 worse than answering once. An external sound verifier helped, but the content of its feedback mattered little; sampling many answers matched it.
numbers: 100 instances, 10-17 nodes. Direct 16%; self-critique 1/100 correct; external verifier about 40%; top-15 sampling with no feedback about 40%. Of 100 optimal colorings the model accepted only 2. In 39 cases it invented same-colour adjacent pairs.
limits: One task, one model, a task with exact checking. Older model.
agent_relevance: A model-only check can destroy right answers. An outside check is useful mostly as a filter on samples.

source: Gou et al. (2023) CRITIC: Large Language Models Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing, arXiv 2305.11738
finding: Gap 3. Critique with tools helped; the same loop without tools did little or hurt.
numbers: ChatGPT HotpotQA F1: CoT 42.8, CRITIC without tool 46.1, CRITIC 52.9. AmbigNQ F1: 64.3 / 67.3 / 74.9. GSM8k: PoT 72.5, without tool 77.0, CRITIC 78.2. text-davinci-003 GSM8k: PoT 70.1, without tool 68.3, CRITIC 72.2. Toxicity (lower is better) ChatGPT: initial 0.325, without tool 0.339, CRITIC 0.173.
limits: Older models. Benchmarks are mostly factual or checkable. No split by item difficulty. Page read to 100000 of 196336 characters.
agent_relevance: Use an outside tool (search, code run, test) as the check step; the model alone is not a reliable questioner.

source: Stav, Berlowitz, Orner & Kraus (2026) When Does Intrinsic Self-Correction Help? A Task-Sensitive Analysis, arXiv 2606.23196
finding: Gaps 3 and 1. Intrinsic self-correction (no outside signal) helped on average with 2026 models, most on verifiable tasks. The gain did not track item difficulty. It did hurt on some tasks, and one model rewrote nearly every answer.
numbers: 5 models. SAT: Mistral 34.62 to 64.96, Haiku 4.5 75.64 to 93.59, Gemini Pro 97.00 to 100. BBEH choice: Haiku 35.00 to 34.50, Mistral 27.75 to 26.50. Correct-to-wrong up to 13.25% (Haiku, BBEH choice), 2.10% max on SAT. Haiku changed its Codenames clue in 98.7% of cases and the score fell. Spearman of gain with baseline accuracy 0.05 (p=0.83); with reasoning intensity 0.54 (p=0.007); with verifiability 0.65 (p<0.001).
limits: Greedy decoding only; LLM-proxy judge scores for the task ratings; no external-feedback arm; no token-matched baseline. Authors expect findings may shift with newer models. Page read to 100000 of 111469 characters.
agent_relevance: Newer models do not fit the 2023 'cannot self-correct' picture on verifiable tasks. Gain depends on how checkable the answer is, not on how hard it is. Always-revise has a cost: 98.7% over-revision in one case.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs (TACL), arXiv 2406.01297
finding: Gap 3. No reviewed work showed success from prompted-LLM feedback except on tasks exceptionally suited to it. Reliable external feedback works. Large-scale fine-tuning can work.
numbers: No pooled numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Only the abstract page was read, not the body. Review ends in 2024.
agent_relevance: Supports putting a tool or test in the check step.

source: Chinn & Brewer (1993) taxonomy of responses to anomalous data, as described in Carmichael et al. (2010) NARST paper; original not opened
finding: Gap 6 partly. Seven responses to anomalous data: ignore; reject; exclude from the theory's domain; hold in abeyance; reinterpret while keeping the theory; reinterpret and make peripheral change; accept and change theory. Only the last is theory change. Four prior-knowledge factors (entrenchment, ontological beliefs, epistemological commitments, background knowledge) and two data factors (credibility, low ambiguity) set the response.
numbers: Secondary study with 71 students in the physical-then-virtual order and 61 in virtual-then-physical. It could not tell which of the seven responses was used. Clear virtual data changed conceptions in about half of students; ambiguous physical data did not cause theory change.
limits: Secondary source. The 1993 original (Review of Educational Research 63, 1-49) was blocked (403 on Illinois and Wiley). No frequencies or tests from the original. Student science data, not experts.
agent_relevance: A richer operator list than preserve vs reframe: reject or discount data, exclude, park (abeyance), reinterpret, patch (peripheral). Abeyance and peripheral patch map to parking an anomaly and editing the frame. Untested on LLMs.

source: When Agents Commit Too Soon: Diagnosing Premature Commitment in LLM Agents, arXiv 2606.22936
finding: Gap 7. Run-to-run agreement of hidden states at step 4 predicts later stability, but stability is not correctness. A commitment prompt made trajectories more stable without raising accuracy.
numbers: Llama-3.1-70B, ReAct on HotpotQA. r=-0.35 between step-4 similarity and trajectory variability; monitor AUROC 0.81 from three partial runs; commitment prompt cut variability 28% against token-matched filler.
limits: Abstract page only. Needs white-box hidden states. The HotpotQA result disappears on hard questions. Authors say the measure cannot show a commitment was premature.
agent_relevance: Warns against using self-agreement as the stop signal: runs can agree and all be wrong.

source: Accurate but Not Humble: Evaluating Epistemic Humility in LLM Agents under Knowledge Conflict, arXiv 2610.12360
finding: Agents notice conflicts early and then drop them. Prompting them to name unresolved conflicts raises escalation but usually costs accuracy.
numbers: Conflict-relevant mentions peak in the first 10% of a trajectory. On TMD, conflict accuracy was 3.0-6.5% vs 39.0-65.0% control (every config more than 30 points lower). Escalate with prompt: GPT-5 on MoNaCo 1.6 to 60.7 while accuracy fell 30.1 to 23.2; BrowseComp 2.8 to 30.8 while 29.4 to 23.5. Qwen-Agent 27B gained on GAIA 53.8 to 76.9.
limits: Four agents, mixed tools and benchmarks. Text read to 100000 of 110000 characters; the appendix prompt was cut off. No exact rate for 'detected then dropped'.
agent_relevance: Supports an open-anomaly list that persists in the state. Also shows that surfacing conflicts can lower accuracy, so the escalation step needs a cost test.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs, arXiv 2501.18585
finding: Gap 1 (cost side). Frequent switching between lines of thought goes with wrong answers. Penalising switches at decoding raised accuracy a little.
numbers: Incorrect responses use 225% more tokens and 418% more thought switches than correct ones. More than 70% of incorrect responses contain at least one correct thought. TIP: AIME24 QwQ-32B 38.3 to 44.1 (+5.8), R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 61.4 to 64.1, DeepSeek-R1 73.8 to 74.8, MATH500-Hard +0.6, GPQA Diamond +1.5.
limits: Math and science multiple choice, open weights, decoding-level fix. Not a reframe test. Switching is not the same as a principled reframe.
agent_relevance: An always-reframe loop may mimic underthinking. Reframe only on a trigger and stay with a line long enough.

source: GEAR: A General Evaluation Framework for Abductive Reasoning, arXiv 2509.24096
finding: Gap 9. Hypothesis diversity can be scored by prediction patterns, not by wording. Diversity and accuracy rose together in training. There is no test of reframes that differ in a stated assumption vs reworded ones.
numbers: 1,500 problems; 9 models; 50,340 hypotheses, 17,835 consistent. 70B-class models give only about 20% consistent hypotheses. Gamma = mean unique predictions per input; beta = mean pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity. Momentum curriculum top-1: Llama-3.1-8B 0.000 to 0.035, Qwen-2.5-7B 0.035 to 0.066, NextCoder-7B 0.025 to 0.065.
limits: Rule-induction puzzles, small models for training, text read to 100000 of 109047 characters. Diversity is in outputs, not in stated assumptions.
agent_relevance: A usable way to check whether two reframes really differ: compare what they predict, not how they are worded.
